newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to plan for new leases on Alaska North Slope.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to plan for new leases on Alaska North Slope.

text.p: The Clinton administration on Tuesday said it would start planning for oil and gas leasing in a portion of a huge federal land reserve on the Alaska's North Slope.

President Clinton has directed U.S. Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt to study the feasibility of new oil and gas drilling in the northeastern corner of the National Petroleum Reserve-Alaska (NPR-A), the Interior Department said.
"The resources of the northeast area of NPR-A have become of greater interest in recent years as oil and gas development approached the reserve's eastern boundary," Babbitt said in a news release.
The 23 million-acre reserve, about 70 miles west of the trans-Alaska pipeline's Prudhoe Bay pump station, has garnered renewed interest from oil companies seeking development frontiers.
In October, three oil companies announced a major oil find on the western border of the reserve.

The Alpine field, estimated to hold 250 million to 300 million recoverable barrels of light crude, is located in the Colville River delta next to the reserve. The field, being developed by Arco Alaska Inc, Anadarko Petroleum Corp and Union Texas Petroleum Holdings Inc, is expected to start production in 2000.
Bob King, press secretary for Gov. Tony Knowles, said Alpine's start-up is likely to make nearby NPR-A development more practical.
"It shows that there is a sizeable (oil deposit) adjacent to this property, but also that the infrastructure is moving in that direction," King said of Alpine.

The Democratic Knowles administration, which has worked for months to convince the Clinton administration to allow new oil development in the petroleum reserve, was pleased with Tuesday's announcement, King said.
"We got what we wanted," he said. "This is very good news. We remain comfortable and committed to the process."
The Knowles administration now wants a lease sale in the area by 1998, he said.
Under Clinton's directive, the U.S. Bureau of Land Management will begin preparing an environmental impact statement for new oil development.
Environmentalists have said they worry about development's inpact on cited certain sites in the reserve used by nesting waterfowl and calving caribou.
But King said those sensistive areas could be avoided by drillers. "I think they can be and should be," he said.
